text: Not everything coming into Castlebridge Logistics is a structured document with fields in known places. Customer emails arrive as free-form text, and warehouse photos may or may not show damage. Classification is for exactly that problem — you don't know what you're looking at yet, so the first job is sorting it into a category.

Document processing, from lesson eight, assumes you know where the data is on the page. Classification is the opposite: it reads free-form input and decides which category it belongs to. For Castlebridge, that's sorting incoming customer emails.

Category classification trains on sample text paired with the category each sample belongs to, stored in a Dataverse table. Castlebridge could train one on past emails tagged Billing, Delivery Status, Damage Claim, and Scheduling. There's also a prebuilt version tuned for general customer feedback categories, usable with no training at all.

The model's output is a category label plus a confidence score, the same shape as lesson eight's extracted fields. The natural next step is almost always a Condition or Switch keyed on that label — route a damage claim to the claims queue, scheduling requests to dispatch. It's the same branching you built in chapter one, just driven by an AI-assigned label instead of a fixed keyword rule.

Images get their own angle on this. Generate description of an image doesn't sort into categories you defined — it looks at a photo and returns a plain-language description plus a list of tags, the same action shape as every other AI Builder step: a file in, structured output out.
Next, lesson ten: taking a longer piece of content and generating an actual written summary with AI Builder and Azure AI.
